title: The Handshake Loan: Why Family and Friends Funding Needs a Paper Trail Before It Becomes a Problem
linkedin:
Every business with a handshake loan in its history looks fine, right up until someone outside the family looks closely.

A parent's deposit. A sibling's fifty thousand dollars. A friend who backed the idea before anyone else would. At the time, writing it up formally feels almost rude, family trusts family, so most of these arrangements stay as a text message or a shared understanding.

The ambiguity doesn't cause a problem in year one. It causes one the day a bank assesses a facility, an investor runs proper diligence, or a buyer's lawyer starts asking questions.

Here's the specific question that trips people up: is that money a gift, a loan, or a stake in the business?

Each one is treated completely differently. A gift generally sits outside the liabilities. A loan belongs on the balance sheet and directly affects how much new debt a bank will extend. A stake means the person who put the money in actually owns part of the business, and that has to show up in the ownership register and any future valuation conversation.

Informal arrangements drift between all three over time, and the owner's version of events doesn't always match the family member's, especially a few years and one rough trading period later.

None of this needs a forty page agreement. A one page document covering the amount, the term, a modest interest rate and the repayment basis, recorded the same way every year, solves it. The cleanest time to do that is months before anyone outside the family needs an answer, not in the middle of a term sheet or a due diligence request.

Quick question for business owners: if a parent, sibling or close friend put money into your business early on, could you say right now whether that was a loan, a gift, or a share of the business?

A lot of owners realise they can't, because it was never written down. It felt unnecessary at the time, family trusts family.

The catch is that a bank, an investor or a buyer will ask that exact question eventually, and "we never really decided" is not an answer any of them can work with.

Worth a one page document now, while there's no deadline attached to it.

A note for business owners across Brisbane, Queensland and the wider East Coast who had family or friends help fund the business in its early days.

It's a common story: a parent's deposit, a sibling's contribution, a friend who believed in the idea before the bank would. At the time, putting it in writing can feel unnecessary between people who trust each other. The difficulty shows up later, when a bank assesses a new facility, an investor looks properly, or a buyer's advisers start asking what every amount on the books actually represents.

The core issue is that this kind of money is usually one of three things, a gift, a loan, or a stake in the business, and each is treated very differently by anyone looking from the outside. Without a simple written record, these arrangements tend to drift between the three over time, and the people involved don't always remember it the same way.

The fix is straightforward and doesn't need to be complicated: a short written agreement covering the amount, the term, a fair interest rate and how it gets repaid, kept consistent year to year. It's a far easier conversation to have now, with no deadline attached, than during a loan application or a sale process later on.

Read the full piece on the ProfitPulse blog for more on getting this right before it becomes a problem.
